candidates.title: HealthFlow: automating electronic health record analysis via a strategically self-evolving multi-agent framework

candidates.abstract: EHRs are a rich source of real-world clinical data, but turning them into valid analyses remains slow and expert-intensive. EHRFlowBench contains analysis tasks derived from 51,280 peer-reviewed papers. Across EHRFlowBench and four established benchmarks, HealthFlow outperforms baselines in generating valid clinical artifacts and completing complex EHR analysis pipelines.
candidates.agent_evidence: Multi-agent framework plans and executes complex EHR analysis pipelines by reusing structured prior analytic experience under dataset/method constraints; explicit research-analysis role and benchmarked workflow completion. Abstract supports multi-step planning and agent collaboration.
candidates.object_evidence: EHR analyses and health data-science tasks derived from 51,280 papers; evaluates validity of clinical analytic artifacts, not simple patient Q&A.
candidates.uncertainties: Need full-text verification of agent role division, tool execution details, and whether benchmark tasks involve concrete clinical objects sufficient for any second module; current 07.03.08 is conservative.

candidates.title: Verification Debt in Automated Biological Research Workflows: A Proof-of-Concept
candidates.authors: Shreya Gopalan; Sundaraparipurnan Narayanan
candidates.abstract: Recent biological research has shown significant interest and progress towards adoption of agentic AI systems. Domain specific agentic platforms with access to large collections of biological tools with code generation and/or querying capabilities, such as Biomni (illustrative case in point), are representative of the capability to orchestrate automated research workflows. Such platforms enable collaborative AI workspace for drug discovery, genomics, bioinformatics, literature research, and experimental planning for biologists and researchers. When such platforms are used for the aforementioned workflows, individually validating every agentic decision and the research process by which it was reached becomes challenging due to the scale of decisions involved and oftentimes, insufficient disclosure of assumptions and methodological choices, limited traceability of evidence, and interpretive judgments embedded throughout the workflow, giving rise to verification debt. Verification debt in agentic environments could result in unexpected failures and consequences in downstream experiments. This study focuses on empirical qualitative characterization of verification debt in agentic (prompt to outcomes) workflows. Biomni was chosen the testing AI agentic platform in this study mainly due to the descriptive traces it provides to track every agentic step. Verification debt is examined through two complementary angles: the individual agentic decision steps that carry claims and evidence, and the underlying research process by which the agent arrives at and reports them. This study attempts to characterize verification debt with 10 test cases (covering proteomics, genomics and drug discovery) with varying degree of biological nuance across three identical and independent runs. Verification debt is represented through 9 decision-step metrics and 13 research-process metrics, and also propose the VERIFY framework for evaluating scientific verifiability and validity in agentic workflows.
candidates.agent_evidence: Uses Biomni as an operative biomedical research agent in 10 proteomics, genomics, and drug-discovery cases across repeated runs; analyzes step-level claims/evidence and research-process traces and proposes VERIFY metrics/framework.

candidates.title: hvantk: an agentic multi-omics framework for variant annotation and analysis
candidates.authors: Enrique Audain; Yasset Perez-Riverol; Marc-Phillip Hitz
candidates.abstract: Large-scale genetic variant analysis involves multiple computational steps, data formats, gene and variant annotation sources and compute requirements. Some of the steps like joint calling for large cohorts are run on large compute clusters, while gene/variant classification algorithms can be run in a desktop computer. At the same time, variant annotations such as gene expression and gene constraints metrics from gnomAD are provided in different formats, by resources that frequently change their versions. Here, we present hvantk, a framework that provides a common data model for large-scale annotation and analysis of genetic variants, by extending popular data formats such as Hail MatrixTable and AnnData. hvantk agentically integrates 21 public multi-omic data providers as plugins that a developer, bioinformatician or an AI agent can author without modifying the framework's core, drives analysis workflows using agent skills, and scales from single desktop computers to high-performance computing clusters. We used hvantk for reanalysing three case-control cohorts, comprising congenital heart disease (CHD), developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (Epi25) and schizophrenia (SCHEMA). Re-ranking of gene-based burden testing results using multi-omic annotations improved the recovery of curated disease genes from 26% to 49% in CHD, 40% to 48% in Epi25 and 51% to 54% in SCHEMA, among the top decile re-ranked genes. Expression at bulk and single-cell levels were the features contributing the most over a baseline of burden, gene constraint and publication count.
candidates.agent_evidence: The framework agentically integrates 21 multi-omic providers, drives analysis workflows using agent skills, and is applied to reanalyze three disease case-control cohorts with gene-burden ranking.
candidates.object_evidence: Genetic variants, multi-omic annotations, and curated disease genes in congenital heart disease, developmental and epileptic encephalopathy, and schizophrenia cohorts.

candidates.title: Auto-MD-bench: Evaluating Autoresearch Agents for Real-World Medical Tasks
candidates.authors: Shenqi Zhou; Qiran Zou; Wenhao Zhao; Zhenyu Liao; Dianbo Liu
candidates.abstract: Autonomous agents are increasingly capable of developing machine learning (ML) models end to end. In medical practice, however, strong performance on the target metric does not fully characterize how good the models are in real-world use cases. For example, medical ML models should also provide well-calibrated risk estimates and remain robust across patient populations. Yet autonomous model development is typically guided by task objectives that emphasize simple predictive discrimination (e.g. AUROC). This raises a key question: are these objectives sufficient to guide agents toward models that meet the broader requirements of real-world medical use? In this study, we introduce Auto-MD-bench, a benchmark of 15 real-world medical tasks from 10 clinical datasets, spanning survival analysis, classification and sequential prediction, with external validation across cohorts, hospitals and time periods. We evaluate four agents: AIDE, AI Scientist v2, Codex, and Autoresearch. The strongest agents achieve competitive primary scores, yet their predicted risks are less calibrated than those of the simple baseline models, which could lead to severe medical accidents. Moreover, models with nearly identical primary scores can exhibit markedly different calibration, while performance varies substantially across population shifts. These findings show that primary task performance alone is insufficient to assess autonomous clinical modeling and multiple different metrics widely used in healthcare practice need to be taken into consideration.
candidates.agent_evidence: Evaluates four autonomous research/model-development agents across complete medical ML task workflows, with external cohort/hospital/time validation and calibration/robustness criteria.
candidates.object_evidence: 15 real-world medical tasks across 10 clinical datasets, including survival, classification, and sequential prediction.

candidates.title: DrugTargetWorld: A Synthetic Biobank for Training and Benchmarking AI Scientists
candidates.authors: Samuel Margolis; Paul Schmiedmayer; Alan Huang; Ethan Chen; Ishan Bhattacharjee; Atman Shah; Ben Viggiano; Fang Cao; Shriya Reddy; Roger Xia; Jack O'Sullivan; Daniel Katz; Matthew Wheeler; Euan Ashley; Bruna Gomes
candidates.abstract: Drug target discovery requires distinguishing molecules that causally drive disease from those that are merely associated with it. Training and evaluating AI agents to perform this workflow end-to-end is difficult because real world biobanks lack known causal ground truth and participant-level data is access controlled. We introduce DrugTargetWorld, a framework that procedurally generates simulated biobanks, or "worlds," with known but concealed causal structure. Each world contains genotypes, proteins, health records, outcomes, and synthetic magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) for 54,000 participants. Agents must construct a disease phenotype, identify causal driver proteins, infer the beneficial direction of modulation, and optionally conduct virtual 'wet lab' experiments. We evaluated nine agents in 540 episodes across 20 cardiovascular worlds and three experimental budgets. Opus 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol achieved the highest mean composite scores, 39.98 and 35.38 of 100, respectively, and both recovered 64% of causal drivers on average. However, no agent reliably distinguished misleading non-causal proteins, and performance remained limited by the integrative judgments required to connect phenotype construction, causal evidence, and intervention decisions. By making each world's causal structure known to the evaluator but hidden from the agent, DrugTargetWorld turns end-to-end drug target discovery into a scalable training and evaluation problem with verifiable reward.
candidates.agent_evidence: Agents construct disease phenotypes, identify causal driver proteins, infer intervention direction, and may run virtual experiments in end-to-end drug-target discovery episodes.
candidates.object_evidence: Synthetic biobank worlds encode genotypes, proteins, health records, outcomes, and MRI for cardiovascular disease target discovery.

candidates.title: Can Coding Agents Build Robust Baselines? A Skill-Based Approach for Automating the Medical Imaging Model-Development Pipeline
candidates.authors: Eugenia Moris; José Ignacio Orlando
candidates.abstract: Developing competitive deep learning baselines for medical imaging remains a highly iterative process requiring literature review, implementation, experimentation, and expert refinement. Existing automation approaches typically optimize isolated components, such as architecture search or hyperparameter tuning, rather than the complete baseline development process. We present an agentic AI Scientist workflow that combines literature-guided reasoning, automated code generation, and hypothesis-driven experimentation to generate competitive baseline models for medical imaging challenges. The framework is evaluated on four public benchmarks spanning segmentation, classification, and detection. Across all tasks, the Experimentation Pipeline consistently improves validation performance, achieving competitive leaderboard results, including 6th place on both PUMA tracks (15 teams) and 31st place on MILK10k (125 teams). On MIDOG25, the resulting model also demonstrates strong domain generalization across scanners, tumor types, and species. Using the same workflow across all challenges without task-specific redesign, we demonstrate that skill-based, literature-guided agentic workflows can substantially reduce the engineering effort required to develop competitive medical imaging baselines.
candidates.agent_evidence: An agentic AI Scientist conducts literature-guided reasoning, code generation, and hypothesis-driven experimentation to build and refine medical-imaging baselines.

candidates.title: NeuroAct: Advancing EEG Analysis and Decoding via Dual-Loop Autonomous Research
candidates.authors: Wei Xiong; Jiangtong Li; Han Zhao; Linxiao Yang; Jie Li; Changjun Jiang
candidates.abstract: EEG analysis and decoding underpin brain-computer interfaces, cognitive assessment, and sleep monitoring. Fixed pipelines and reward-driven search do not explicitly determine how signal structure, representations, predictor behavior, and training dynamics contribute to performance or generalization gaps, leaving intervention choice underdetermined. We introduce NeuroAct, an autonomous research agent framework for EEG analysis and decoding. NeuroAct implements dual-loop autonomous research across EEG foundation models, task-specific predictors, and model combinations. In an inner loop, research, development, and review roles use evidence on signal structure, representations, predictor behavior, and training dynamics to test hypotheses, select analyses or interventions, and refine candidates using performance, stability, and cost feedback. An outer loop distills outcomes into conditional, testable recommendations with task and model conditions, then validates and revises them on subsequent tasks.We evaluate four settings: (A) EEG General Analysis, (B) Cross-task Model Optimization, (C) Single-task Open Research, and (D) Collaborative Prediction. In Setting A, NeuroAct's 80.88 macro-average exceeds BrainAgent's 63.13 by 17.75 points. In Setting B, NeuroAct raises EEGPT's mean balanced accuracy (BA) by 7.34 points and HBN Pearson's (r) from 0.6894 to 0.7362; in Setting C, it improves ADFTD BA by 16.33 points; and in Setting D, it raises Workload BA from 79.69% to 85.02%. Experience reuse raises BCIC-IV-2a BA from 34.66% to 50.81% while reducing LLM tokens by 64.02%, indicating recommendations improve cross-task performance. NeuroAct enables evidence-guided EEG research improved by cross-task experience.
candidates.agent_evidence: Explicit autonomous EEG research framework with inner-loop role coordination, evidence-guided hypotheses/interventions, feedback-based candidate refinement, and outer-loop reusable recommendations.

candidates.title: TCMScience: An Autonomous Scientist for Traditional Chinese Medicine
candidates.authors: Yanlan Kang; Ruiqi Liu; Xinpei Gu; Tzu-Yi Lei; Shuai Xu; Xukun Zhang; William Cheng-Chung Chu
candidates.abstract: Traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) research connects classical texts, medicinal entities, molecular assays, computational predictions, and clinical studies. An autonomous research agent must preserve the inferential boundaries between these evidence types while coordinating analysis across heterogeneous resources. We introduce TCMScience, a scientific knowledge-discovery agent that separates language-model proposals from execution and release authority. Its architecture combines a trusted kernel, a scientific compiler, and claim-support contracts: plans are compiled into typed operations, execution is bounded by explicit permissions, and candidate findings are checked against source provenance, study design, and claim scope before release. The full capability registry contains 117 public-source connectors with 444 typed operations across 29 domains and 150 native tools across 12 domains; the TCM data hub catalogs 136 databases, 76 dataset specifications, and 84,294 formula-source records. These resources support model-independent workflows through browser and local execution interfaces. In a network-pharmacology analysis of Gegen Qinlian Tang, replacing the whole-proteome background with the assayed-protein background changed the number of significant pathways from 66 to zero; incorporating inactive screening records identified nine pathways, including drug-metabolism signals retained as mechanistic hypotheses. A governance ablation over 121 constructed erroneous outputs spanning 26 classes released 121 errors without governance, 57 with the domain layer, seven with the kernel, and zero with both layers. All 10 compliant controls were retained. These results establish complementary control of known failure modes and show how explicit evidence contracts change the conclusions an agent is permitted to report.
candidates.agent_evidence: Autonomous scientist plans and executes bounded knowledge-discovery operations, checks claims against source provenance/study design, and performs a biomedical pathway analysis with governance ablations.

candidates.title: An immune world model for multiscale forecasting and therapeutic hypothesis generation
candidates.authors: Taoyong Cui; Xi Wang; Zonghang Li; Jinchao Ding; Lingsen You; Yuzhi Xu; Wanghan Xu; Fang Wu; Kejun Ying; Wanli Ouyang; Pheng Ann Heng; Ling Yang; Zhenfei Yin; Yingcheng Wu
candidates.abstract: Immune therapies act across cell-intrinsic programs, tissue ecosystems, and patient-specific immune states, yet most predictors address these scales separately. We used a governed evolutionary AI Scientist to construct the Immune World Model, an action-conditioned model that learns how interventions move immune states across cellular, tissue, and individual levels. The Immune World Model--building Scientist searched candidate architectures and workflows, and the resulting world model was frozen before independent confirmation. The frozen model generalized to unseen interventions and biological contexts, recovered intervention-specific cellular programs, integrated cell and tissue information to improve ecosystem and patient-response prediction, and forecast unseen perturbation combinations. Immune World Model--guided analysis then combined measured perturbations with cross-axis inference to nominate IL-36$γ$ plus SIRP$α$ inhibition as a complementary-axis therapeutic hypothesis, whereas a governed self-correction audit rejected every screened cytokine pair. The Immune World Model provides a framework for multiscale immune simulation that connects AI Scientist-driven model construction, intervention forecasting, and the generation of prospectively testable therapeutic hypotheses.
candidates.agent_evidence: A governed AI Scientist searches architectures/workflows to construct a biological world model; the resulting model forecasts interventions and supports a therapeutic hypothesis tested through a self-correction audit.
